title: Grade 6 Science — Fri, May 21
description: Food: Where Does It Come From? — Day 5 of 5: Synthesis and reasoning
subject: science

questions.question: If all plants on Earth suddenly disappeared, animals would die within a few weeks. Explain WHY.
options: Animals need the shade plants provide
Plants are the foundation of all food chains — no plants means no food for herbivores, then no food for carnivores, and no oxygen from photosynthesis
Animals need plants only for shelter
Animals would adapt to eat rocks instead
questions.explanation: Plants are producers — base of every food chain. No plants = no herbivore food → herbivores die → carnivores die. Plus plants produce the oxygen all animals breathe.

questions.question: A farmer grows only one crop (monoculture) for many years. Soil nutrients deplete. The BEST solution is:
options: Add more water to soil
Crop rotation — alternating crops including legumes to replenish nitrogen; different crops use different nutrients
Remove all weeds immediately
Plant the same crop but more densely
questions.explanation: Monoculture depletes specific nutrients. Crop rotation: different crops use/restore different nutrients; legumes fix nitrogen. This maintains soil health without chemical fertilisers.

questions.question: Bees are essential to food production not because they are a food source, but because:
options: Bees eat pests that damage crops
Bees pollinate flowers — without pollination, most fruits and seeds cannot form
Bees provide fertiliser
Bees remove weeds
questions.explanation: About 75% of food crops depend on animal pollination (mainly bees). Without bees to carry pollen between flowers, these plants cannot produce fruits or seeds — devastating food production.

questions.question: Why can we eat the stem of sugarcane raw, but the stem of a potato plant is toxic?
options: All stems are the same
Different plants store different chemicals — sugarcane stems store sucrose (harmless sugar); potato stems contain solanine (toxic alkaloid)
Potato stem just tastes bitter but is safe
Sugarcane is a grass, so different rules apply
questions.explanation: Sugarcane stores sucrose in its stem — sweet and edible. Potato leaves and stems contain solanine (toxic). Only the underground tuber (stem) is safe.

questions.question: In a food web: Grass → Grasshopper → Frog → Snake → Eagle. If grasshoppers are poisoned by pesticide, predict what happens to the eagle population:
options: Eagle population increases because predators are gone
Eagle population declines — grasshoppers gone → frogs starve → snakes starve → eagles have less food
Eagle population is unaffected since eagles eat snakes not grasshoppers
Nothing changes
questions.explanation: Food chains are interconnected. Loss of grasshoppers cascades up: frogs starve → fewer snakes → eagles have less food → eagle numbers decline. This is trophic cascade.

questions.question: Farmers spray pesticides on crops. Pesticide concentrations are: Soil=1 unit, Grass=10 units, Grasshopper=100 units, Bird=1000 units. This phenomenon is called:
options: Food chain pollution
Biomagnification — pesticides concentrate at higher trophic levels because they are not broken down and accumulate
Photosynthesis reversal
Nutrient cycling
questions.explanation: Biomagnification: pesticides accumulate in fat tissue and are not excreted. Each animal eats many of the organisms below it, so the concentration multiplies at each trophic level.

questions.question: Why is it more energy-efficient to eat plants directly than to eat animals that ate plants?
options: Plants taste better
Only 10% of energy is transferred between trophic levels — eating plants gives 10x more food energy per unit of sunlight
Animals are bigger so harder to catch
Plants are free while animals cost money
questions.explanation: Eating grass directly = 100% of plant energy available. Eating a cow that ate grass = only 10% (90% was lost as heat in the cow). Plant-based diets extract far more energy from the same land.

questions.question: We eat carrots for beta-carotene (converted to Vitamin A). Cooking carrots INCREASES beta-carotene availability. Why?
options: Heat creates Vitamin A from water
Cooking breaks down cell walls, releasing bound beta-carotene and making it more accessible for absorption
Raw carrots have no beta-carotene
Cooking adds vitamins from the pot
questions.explanation: Beta-carotene is trapped in plant cell walls. Cooking softens/breaks down cell walls, releasing more beta-carotene. Adding a little fat further increases absorption (fat-soluble vitamin).

questions.question: A student says: 'Potatoes are roots, like carrots.' Is this correct? Explain.
options: Correct — both are underground so both are roots
Incorrect — carrot is a root; potato is a stem tuber (modified stem with 'eyes' that are nodes)
Correct — underground = root always
Incorrect — potato is a fruit
questions.explanation: Carrot is a taproot (has no 'eyes', grows from root tissue). Potato is a stem tuber — 'eyes' are axillary buds, proving it's stem tissue. Underground location doesn't make something a root.

questions.question: Organic farming uses no synthetic fertilisers or pesticides. Food from organic farms is grown using:
options: Nothing — organic means no inputs at all
Compost, manure, crop rotation, and biological pest control — natural methods only
Only water and sunlight
Genetically modified seeds only
questions.explanation: Organic farming uses natural inputs: compost/manure for nutrients, crop rotation for soil health, companion planting and beneficial insects for pest control.

questions.question: Forest tribes traditionally eat hundreds of different plant species. Modern diets depend on just ~20 major crops. The risk of depending on few crops is:
options: No risk — fewer crops are easier to manage
If one major crop fails (disease, drought), food security is devastated — biodiversity provides resilience
More crops mean more work for farmers only
Variety is less nutritious than few crops
questions.explanation: Ireland's potato famine (1845) showed the danger — one crop failure caused massive starvation. Crop biodiversity is insurance against failures.

questions.question: A mushroom (fungus) can grow on a dead log but NOT on a live, healthy tree. Why?
options: Live trees are too tall for mushrooms
Mushrooms (saprophytes) need dead/decaying organic matter — live trees have intact cells and defences that prevent saprophytic fungi from decomposing them
Mushrooms prefer sunlight which dead logs provide
Live trees are poisonous to fungi
questions.explanation: Saprophytic fungi need dead, broken-down cells to grow on. Live plants have intact cell walls, immune defences, and antimicrobial compounds. Parasitic fungi (different from saprophytes) can infect live plants.

questions.question: In the food chain: Sunlight → Rice plant → Rat → Snake → Eagle. If the eagle is at trophic level 5, the rat is at:
options: Level 1
Level 2
Level 3
Level 4
questions.explanation: Sunlight is not a trophic level. Rice = Level 1 (producer). Rat = Level 2? No: Rice(1)→Rat(2)→Snake(3)→Eagle(4). So rat is at trophic level 2 = primary consumer.

questions.question: Fermentation (making curd, bread, wine) relies on microorganisms to change food. This means:
options: Microorganisms only destroy food
Microorganisms can be beneficial food sources and food transformers, not just harmful pathogens
Fermented food is always dangerous
Only bacteria can ferment food
questions.explanation: Bacteria (Lactobacillus for curd), yeasts (for bread and wine), and moulds (for cheese) transform raw materials into new foods with different nutrition and flavour profiles. Microorganisms are vital food partners.

questions.question: A climate scientist predicts: 'As oceans warm, phytoplankton (tiny ocean plants) will decrease.' This is alarming because:
options: Phytoplankton taste good
Phytoplankton are the BASE of ocean food chains — their decline cascades to fish, seabirds, and global oxygen production
Warmer oceans are good for all sea life
Phytoplankton only affect land plants
questions.explanation: Marine phytoplankton produce ~50% of Earth's oxygen AND are the foundation of all ocean food chains. Their decline would devastate ocean ecosystems and affect global climate and food supply.
